t: Maximum Number of Robots Within Budget — Sliding Window with Monotonic Deque
o: We need the longest contiguous window whose cost max(chargeTimes) + k·sum(runningCosts) fits the budget. Brute force over all windows is O(n²). Since cost isn't monotone in window growth in a simple way, we use the standard pattern: expand right, shrink left while over budget, tracking the window max with a monotonic deque and window sum with prefix sums. In example 1, window [3,6,1] costs 6 + 3·6 = 24 <= 25, giving answer 3.
k: Sliding window works because shrinking never hurts: if a window is unaffordable, all its supersets ending later are too.
A monotonic decreasing deque gives O(1) amortized window-max updates as both ends move.
Prefix sums make window running-cost queries O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: Two Pointers + Monotonic Deque + Prefix Sum
a.i: Maintain window [l, r]. Push chargeTimes[r] onto a deque keeping values decreasing (pop smaller backs). While current cost exceeds budget, pop the front if it equals chargeTimes[l] and advance l. Record r-l+1 as a candidate answer whenever the window is valid. Each index enters and leaves the deque once, so total time is linear.
s: For each r: push r maintaining decreasing order of chargeTimes in the deque.
While maxCharge + (r-l+1)*(windowSum) > budget, shrink from the left (pop front if stale).
a.t: O(n) — each index pushed/popped from the deque at most once; pointer l moves monotonically.

w: Watch out for overflow: k up to 5e4 times sums up to 5e9 needs 64-bit math everywhere. A common pitfall is checking affordability before pushing r, or failing to pop the deque front exactly when it leaves the window. Alternative: binary search on the answer length combined with the same window check (O(n log n)) — mention it if asked. Note the window can become empty (answer 0), as in example 2.
